system_prompt:
You are a medical language simplification assistant. Convert the following clinical discharge summary into simple, plain Indian English for the patient's family members.

Rules:
1. Keep every medical term but immediately explain it in plain words in parentheses on first use only, e.g. 'hypertension (high BP)'. Keep explanations short (under 6-8 words per term).
2. Use simple language a 6th-grader can understand. Avoid unexplained jargon. Use common Indian English terms where natural: 'sugar' for diabetes, 'BP' for blood pressure, 'motions' for bowel movements.
3. Preserve ALL factual information — never add, remove, alter, or infer any clinical facts, values, dates, or instructions.
4. Write as continuous plain prose paragraphs — no bullet points, no headers, no numbered lists. Output only the simplified text, nothing else.
5. CONCISENESS & LENGTH CONSTRAINT (CRITICAL): The simplified text must be concise and proportionate, strictly between 1.2x and 2.0x the word length of the original source report. Do NOT over-expand. Never list hypothetical normal ranges or unmentioned medical conditions. Only mention normal ranges for tests/vitals explicitly recorded in the document.
6. Use a calm, respectful tone. Do not add emotional commentary, opinions, or reassurances not present in the original text.
7. CRITICAL — person and tense: First check whether the summary records the patient's death (look for 'death', 'expired', 'deceased', 'asystole', 'absence of pulse', 'body released', or similar). If yes, write in third person past tense for the family ('the patient', 'he/she/they'). If no, address the patient directly in second person ('you', 'your').
8. CRITICAL — dates: Convert dates exactly as they appear using the format specified in the document. Never guess or infer a date not explicitly stated.
9. For each medication, state its name and brief purpose in plain language, e.g. 'Ceftriaxone — an antibiotic to fight infection'.
10. For each procedure or device, briefly state what it is and why it was done, e.g. 'haemodialysis (machine filtering waste when kidneys could not)'.
11. If the text contains placeholders such as {omitted} or [person], reproduce them exactly as they appear. Do not guess or replace them.
12. DOMAIN GUARDRAIL: You are exclusively a medical simplification assistant. Output only the simplified clinical explanation.

output_text:
You were admitted on 09/19/2022 and discharged on 10/19/2022 after staying for 1 month 11 hours in a ward, with payment through SUS. You are a 60‑year‑old female, living at [address], with incomplete high school education and working as a cleaner. Your estimated weight was 60 kg, predicted weight 57 kg, and height 164 cm.

During this stay you had several serious problems. You had a resolved septic shock (dangerous infection causing low blood pressure) that started in the lungs (pulmonary focus), acute respiratory failure (trouble breathing), hypotension (low BP), and a decreased level of consciousness (less awake). A blood culture (test for germs in blood) grew staphylococcus aureus (type of bacteria) oxas (oxacillin) and you also had a coronavirus infection (COVID‑19) confirmed by rtPCR (viral test) on 03/15. You developed an acute kidney injury (kidney damage) classified as KDIGO 1 (mild) that was pre‑renal (due to low blood flow) but later resolved. Your liver cirrhosis (scarring of the liver) caused a pleural effusion (fluid around the lung) that needed both paracentesis (draining fluid from the abdomen) and thoracentesis (draining fluid from the chest) for relief.

On 09/19 you had a blood gas showing a pH of 1.61 (acid‑base measure), albumin 0.49 g/dL (low protein), serum albumin 2.1 g/dL, glucose 164 mg/dL, LDH 72 U/L (enzyme level), and serum LDH 314 U/L. A thoracentesis (chest fluid drain) on the same day showed transudate (thin fluid) with protein 2 g/dL, serum protein 7.7 g/dL, LDH 72 U/L, serum LDH 279 U/L, pH 7.378, albumin 0.61 g/dL, serum albumin 1.9 g/dL, amylase 117 U/L, glucose 183 mg/dL, and a negative culture (no germs). On 09/23/2022 you drained 700 ml of transudate, on 10/06/2022 you drained 1000 ml, on 10/10/2022 another 1000 ml, and on 10/15/2022 a further 1000 ml.

Your current illness began when [person] was diagnosed with liver cirrhosis of unclear cause, to be clarified later at the gastroclinic at [organization]. On 02/09/2022 you were advised to increase furosemide (diuretic to remove fluid) to 40 mg twice daily and spironolactone (potassium‑sparing diuretic) to 50 mg daily because of massive ascites (abdominal fluid), dyspnea (shortness of breath), and weight gain. A paracentesis (abdomen fluid drain) on that day removed 4.1 liters of fluid, and another on 13/09 removed 1.4 liters.

You were referred from the emergency unit with a report that you were admitted on 18/09/2022 with 85 % oxygen saturation on room air, obtunded (very sleepy), peripheral cyanosis (bluish skin) and livedo reticularis (mottled skin), and you were intubated (tube placed in airway) without problems. {omitted} noted that you developed dyspnea that morning. Four ampoules of furosemide were given but you produced no urine, according to the transport team. I admitted you intubated, sedated with midazolam (sleep‑inducing medicine) and fentanyl (pain medicine), paralyzed with rocuronium (muscle relaxant), and supported with norepinephrine (medicine to raise BP) at 20 ml/h.

Initially you were in {omitted}, where doctors thought your acute respiratory failure might be due to coronavirus, congestion, or lung infection (sepsis of pulmonary focus). Empirical ceftriaxone (antibiotic to fight infection) was started and a diagnostic paracentesis was done, which showed no spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (infection of abdominal fluid). On the same day a thoracentesis removed 1000 ml of transudate, and a relief paracentesis removed 4000 ml; albumin (protein given to keep fluid in vessels) was given because of the large fluid removal. A point‑of‑care ultrasound (pocus) on 09/19 showed lines and pleural thickening, supporting the lung infection theory.

Because the blood culture grew staphylococcus aureus, clarithromycin (antibiotic) and clindamycin (antibiotic) were added on 09/24, and the antibiotic regimen was changed from ceftriaxone + clarithromycin to levofloxacin (antibiotic) + oxacillin (antibiotic) as directed by the [organization]. An echocardiogram (heart ultrasound) was ordered to look for endocarditis (infection of heart lining) because of the bacteria in the blood. On the morning of 09/27, antibiotics were escalated to meropenem (strong antibiotic) + oxacillin because CRP (inflammation marker) rose and more vasoactive drugs were needed.

Your breathing improved, you were taken off the ventilator (extubated) on 10/03, and supplemental oxygen was stopped on 10/13. The septic condition resolved and the antibiotic course finished on 10/08. You stayed in the hospital because you needed 24‑hour nursing
